video_title: With Buybacks Ending, A Market Correction Is Not Off The Table | Lance Roberts
gist: Lance Roberts tells Adam Taggart that a 10-20% market decline looks unlikely near-term, but the combined drag of the corporate buyback blackout window, quarter-end rebalancing, and a record options expiration make a 3-5% correction to the 50/100-day moving average plausible before the midterms; he lays out his CAPE-vs-PEG valuation framework (a 40x-earnings market implies a -2.6% projected 10-year passive return), argues retail investors structurally cannot compete with headline-reading trading algorithms, and walks through Fed/Treasury mechanics, the DSA's midterm momentum, and why revaluing US gold reserves would be fiscal 'accounting theater' rather than a real fix.

insights.claim: Starting the day of this taping, the corporate buyback blackout window begins, meaning companies won't be adding buying support to the market for several weeks even though they aren't selling, which leaves the market more vulnerable to headline, geopolitical, and general concern-driven risk during that stretch.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A known, calendar-based reduction in a key source of market demand — a mechanical reason to expect thinner support and more headline sensitivity over the following weeks.
insights.quote: the blackout window begins for corporate buybacks

insights.claim: Lance's base case: a 10-20% market decline looks unlikely because that risk is being 'rung out' via ongoing sideways consolidation, but a correction of 3-5% back to the 50-day or 100-day moving average is not off the table given the buyback blackout, quarter-end rebalancing, and the largest third-Friday options expiration on record this month.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable near-term market call with magnitude and technical levels (50-day/100-day moving average) that can be tracked directly against price action.
insights.quote: expecting a 10, 15, 20% decline. I think that's getting rung out of the market because of this consolidation, but a correction back to the 50-day moving average, maybe the 100 day moving average, which would be 3 to 5%.

insights.claim: Market breadth is weakening again after improving earlier in the year: the equal-weight S&P (RSP) is underperforming the cap-weighted index, and on the day of taping semiconductors/Nvidia are up while the broader market is down, consistent with a narrow, concentration-driven rally rather than broad participation.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Deteriorating breadth is a classic technical warning sign that a rally is increasingly dependent on a handful of mega-cap/semiconductor names — worth monitoring RSP-vs-SPY relative performance as a leading risk indicator.
insights.quote: RSP has been underperforming. Um we've seen you know underperforming a bit, right? So I just suggest there's some weakness and take a if you take a look at the heat map today is a good example.

insights.claim: Because put options are so unpopular right now ('nobody wants puts'), downside insurance is unusually cheap; Lance's firm has been adding S&P puts in their options-based portfolio sleeve and plans to add more, alongside raising cash, shifting bond duration, and taking some profits, explicitly to hedge downside volatility risk until the market gets through the midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A directly actionable, timed hedging idea: buying index puts is currently cheap precisely because sentiment is complacent — a tactical opportunity for portfolio protection into a known volatility catalyst (midterms).
insights.quote: that insurance is very cheap. And yes, um we've been dollar cost averaging a bit

insights.claim: Lance cites Goldman Sachs' year-end S&P 500 target near 8,000 and Fundstrat's Mark Newton's similar ~8,000 target, both of whom expect volatility between now and the midterms followed by a stronger advance afterward; Lance's own firm's year-end target is 7,900.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Gives concrete, comparable year-end index price targets from multiple sources for benchmarking against actual year-end outcomes.
insights.quote: right now Goldman's got an 8,000 target.

themes.theme: Fed Policy, Jobs Data & Treasury Mechanics

insights.claim: August payrolls beat expectations at 162,000 (described as a 'four-sigma beat') with a positive revision to July's previously negative print, but Lance notes the normal monthly labor-force replacement rate is about 200,000, so even this 'beat' reflects underlying labor-market weakness rather than strength.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A useful corrective to headline-driven 'good jobs number' narratives: the print still falls short of the replacement rate needed to keep pace with labor-force growth.
insights.quote: replacement rate on a monthly basis is about 200. So, even at 162, this is a very weak number economic growth wise.

insights.claim: Year-over-year wage growth decelerated to 3.1% from 3.2% in the prior report, implying real wage growth is close to zero — a more informative underlying signal than the payroll headline about the state of the economy.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Near-zero real wage growth undercuts the bullish read on the headline jobs beat and matters directly for consumer spending/discretionary-sector earnings estimates.
insights.quote: wage growth on a year-over-year basis decline, the 3.1% from 3.2% last report. So, wages are in a continual decline here.

insights.claim: Lance flags that August payroll strength is seasonally inflated by back-to-school hiring (teachers, bus drivers, cafeteria staff returning to work), and this seasonal boost does not necessarily carry over into September's data.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A specific seasonal-adjustment caveat for interpreting the August jobs print — don't extrapolate August strength into a September/Q4 trend without adjustment.
insights.quote: this is also August. What happens in August? All the teachers go back to work.

insights.claim: Lance predicts Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will neither hike nor cut rates in the near term, instead waiting for more data, because current inflationary pressures (an oil price spike, tariffs) are transient, and hiking into transient inflation risks having to reverse course later, which would undermine confidence in his monetary policy.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A specific near-term Fed-policy call (hold, not hike or cut) tied to an explicit rationale about transient inflation drivers — useful for positioning rate-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: I don't think he hikes rates. I don't think he cuts rates. I think he acknowledges the data and says we want to see a little bit more data first before we make a decision.

insights.claim: Warsh reportedly wants the Fed to stop signaling policy directly and let markets set signals instead (reversing roughly 15 years of heavy Fed forward guidance), but continued public dovish-leaning comments from Fed officials like Waller undermine that reset, creating a tension Lance sees as part of why markets are so volatile lately.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A structural explanation for elevated market volatility: an internal Fed communication-strategy conflict (silence vs. leakage) is itself a source of noise for traders parsing every Fed official's public remarks.
insights.quote: The markets are trying to wean themselves off of having this signal from the Fed, but then you have these speakers coming out giving signals from the Fed, which I'm surprised

insights.claim: The Treasury's recently started small-scale debt operation (buying longer paper, issuing shorter paper, roughly $4 billion to start but could grow) is routine balance-sheet management to reduce the government's future interest cost, not a deliberate attempt by Treasury Secretary Bessent to manipulate rates down as some commentary suggested; the real driver pushing the term premium up is roughly 50 hedge funds using leveraged basis trades (owning 8.5% of the Treasury market) shorting heavily against Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Reframes a widely-discussed 'Bessent is manipulating rates' narrative as routine debt management, while identifying the actual mechanical driver (leveraged hedge-fund basis trades) of elevated term premium — and flags a potential future bond short-squeeze trade once those positions have to unwind (though Lance says it's too early to trade it).
insights.quote: we've got basically 50 hedge funds that own eight and a half% of the treasury market and they're shoving interest rates around because of basically they're leveraging that treasury play.

themes.theme: Valuation Framework: CAPE, PEG, and Why Buy-and-Hold Is Risky at 40x

insights.claim: Lance states plainly that he is not a fan of buy-and-hold investing at current valuations (~40x earnings); using CAPE-based math, an investor who is 50 today and retires at 65, investing today at 40x earnings, faces a projected -2.6% annualized rate of return over the next 10 years — effectively a decade of no real progress from passive index investing at current prices.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified argument against blind buy-and-hold index investing at current valuations — directly actionable for retirement-timeline investors deciding on asset allocation today.
insights.quote: valuations are at 40 times earnings today. What does that tell us about future? If I'm 50 today and I'm going to retire at 65 and I'm investing today at 40 times earnings, that's a negative point negative 2.6% rate of return over the next 10 years based on those valuations.

insights.claim: Lance distinguishes CAPE (a backward-looking earnings valuation measure, currently showing an 'expensive' 40x market) from PEG (price-to-earnings-growth, a forward-looking measure), noting the market is technically the cheapest it's been on a PEG basis in about 20 years given very optimistic analyst forward earnings-growth estimates — but that this can flip to 'extremely expensive very quickly' if a recession or earnings shock hits and those growth estimates get cut.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A dual-lens valuation framework: current 'cheap on PEG' readings are entirely conditional on realized future earnings growth — a single catalyst (recession, capex pullback) could flip the market from cheap to expensive almost overnight.
insights.quote: analysts are very optimistic over the next couple of years about very strong earnings growth. The market is technically cheap on the the earnings growth estimates over the next two years due to the economy, due to capex spending

insights.claim: Nvidia is cited as the poster child for the PEG framework: a couple of years ago its PEG ratio looked 'extremely high' and the stock was called too expensive, but because it met or exceeded aggressive earnings-growth expectations, the same stock now trades at an extremely cheap PEG ratio.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A real-world case study showing how growth-adjusted valuation multiples can look completely different from headline P/E, and why extrapolating Nvidia's realized growth forward is the market's key implicit bet.
insights.quote: A couple of years ago, the PEG ratio for Nvidia was extremely high

insights.claim: At current elevated valuations, Lance argues quality fixed income (roughly 5% yields on corporates/Treasuries) or dividend-yielding equities (~2-2.5% yield plus equity growth) offer a better locked-in return profile than the projected -2.6% return from passive index buy-and-hold, provided the investor also actively manages portfolio risk (adjusting exposure up/down) rather than pure buy-and-hold.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: An explicit, actionable asset-allocation alternative to passive equity indexing at these valuation levels — favoring bonds and dividend equities with active risk management.
insights.quote: If I can buy bonds paying five 5% on average right now, either corporates or treasuries, and I can lock in a 5% rate of return over the next 10 years, that's a hell of a lot better than a negative 2.6.

insights.claim: Lance identifies retail investors' lack of a disciplined sell process (versus a well-thought-out buy process) as a core recurring mistake — investors accumulate positions they no longer have a thesis for and hold both losers (loss aversion) and winners (anchoring to ever-higher price targets) without a plan, which is a primary value a professional adviser or systematic weekly portfolio review process adds.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A practical diagnostic for retail investors: if you can't articulate your sell discipline for every position, you're structurally prone to underperformance regardless of your buy skill.
insights.quote: put a lot of thought into getting in but not a lot of thought into getting out.

insights.claim: Investor psychology drivers cited: 'anchoring' (fixating on a peak portfolio value or a specific share price target, e.g. wanting to hold until $100/share becomes wanting $200 once it's hit) and Kahneman's prospect theory (the pain of a loss is felt roughly twice as intensely as the pleasure of an equivalent gain) together explain panic-selling and chasing behavior; Lance recommends clients anchor to their portfolio value from three years ago rather than yesterday's high-water mark to make better-calibrated decisions.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable anti-anchoring technique (benchmark against a multi-year-ago portfolio value, not yesterday's peak) that investors can apply directly to reduce panic-driven trading errors.
insights.quote: people feel the pain of a loss twice as much emotionally as they feel the joy of a gain.

themes.theme: Algorithmic Trading Structurally Disadvantages Retail Investors

insights.claim: By the time a retail investor finishes reading a single macro headline (e.g., a jobs report print), systematic/algorithmic trading systems have already parsed the data, modeled implications for forward earnings, Fed policy, and geopolitics, and executed trades across multiple asset classes (stocks, currencies, gold) within milliseconds.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Concrete mechanistic explanation for why headline-driven day-trading is a losing game for retail investors — informs Lance's practical advice to wait for the algo-driven initial move to play out before acting.
insights.quote: By the time you read that, these systemic algorithms have already read the headline, analyzed the data, looked at forward returns on earnings, estimated future projections on earnings growth based on this data, what Fed policy might be, what geopolitical policy might be from that headline, and then have already placed trades across multiple asset classes

insights.claim: Lance cites two real examples of headline-driven, non-fundamental price action: Palantir sold off 4% on a Google-defense-AI headline, then Palo Alto Networks jumped 10% the next day purely on an earnings headline — illustrating that daily stock moves are frequently disconnected from underlying fundamentals and instead driven by algorithmic reaction to news flow.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A cautionary, concrete illustration for investors tempted to react emotionally to single-day price swings in individual names — the move often reflects algo/headline noise, not a fundamental thesis change.
insights.quote: two days ago, Palent, there's a headline out about Google getting into the defense AI space. Palunteer sells off 4%. The next day, there's a a earnings report that comes out from PaloAlto Networks and the stock's up 10%.

insights.claim: Lance's explicit advice: retail investors should not try to compete with high-frequency/systematic trading on speed; instead, when a market-moving headline hits, wait for the algorithmic initial reaction to play out and let the market stabilize before taking any action, since the market often measures and corrects the accuracy of that initial algo-driven move.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A directly actionable behavioral rule for retail investors reacting to news: pause and observe rather than immediately trade off a fresh headline.
insights.quote: wait and let the markets just react to it and then see where the market stabilizes.

insights.claim: Fidelity data shows a record roughly 800,000 '401(k) millionaire' accounts (about 3% of Fidelity's 28.5 million total 401k accounts), but the median 401(k) balance is only $32,000-$34,000 — the reported average balance of ~$155,000 is heavily skewed upward by that top 3% of accounts.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A stark illustration of how concentrated US retirement wealth actually is — headline 'record millionaire' and 'average balance' statistics dramatically overstate the typical American's retirement readiness.
insights.quote: Fidelity manages 28.5 million 401k plans.

insights.claim: Structural reforms intended to help retail investors — decimalized stock pricing (2000) and the elimination of trading commissions — instead removed 'roadblocks' to trading frequency, and decades of academic studies consistently show frequent traders underperform buy-and-hold, which Lance argues has net reduced the economic prosperity of most Americans while benefiting Wall Street.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A structural, historically-grounded argument that 'democratizing' trading access (free trades, real-time quotes) has net harmed average investors by encouraging overtrading — relevant context for evaluating any new retail-trading product or app.
insights.quote: study after study after study tells you that if you trade often, you are going to wind up underperforming the market because you're going to lose more than you make on your trades most of the time.

themes.theme: Midterm Elections, Policy Risk, and the DSA

insights.claim: Lance assigns a 'decently high probability' that Republicans lose the House in the midterms (Democrats need only four additional seats to flip it) while Republicans likely retain the Senate, producing a split Congress that would create political gridlock — which he notes Wall Street would actually favor (gridlock is historically good for stocks) even though it would stall the Trump administration's economic agenda.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A specific political-risk call with a direct market implication: a split Congress (gridlock) is framed as a net positive for equities even if it complicates the administration's legislative agenda.
insights.quote: I think there's a decent risk that the House flips, the the the Senate remains the same. That's going to give us political gridlock, even more so than we have now

insights.claim: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has real fundraising momentum heading into the midterms — cited example: AOC's primary opponent significantly outraised her rival — and Democratic candidates have broadly outraised Republican candidates in many races, which Lance flags as a real (not merely rhetorical) political-momentum risk factor to monitor.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Fundraising momentum data is presented as a more reliable signal than unreliable polling for gauging which political forces are gaining ground before the midterms.
insights.quote: Democratic Socialist Movement, the DSA, they've got a lot of momentum going.

insights.claim: Lance predicts that within roughly the next three weeks, the administration will likely pursue some new Iran-related negotiation or de-escalation move, given the persistent political linkage between gas prices, the Iran situation, and voter sentiment ahead of the midterms; he also floats (with skepticism about its likelihood) a scenario where the government directly subsidizes gas prices or sends consumer rebate checks — inflationary but politically popular timed just before the election.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, time-boxed catalyst (Iran-related headline within ~3 weeks) and a low-probability but market-relevant inflationary policy tail-risk (gas subsidies/rebates) to watch for ahead of the midterms.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised to see a new negotiation starting to happen uh to try to get a little bit of leverage going into the election.

insights.claim: Lance states his personal view (explicitly flagged as opinion, not analysis) that 'socialism is not the answer' and that capitalism is the model that has brought the greatest prosperity to the greatest number of people in history, while acknowledging capitalism today is not running perfectly and the focus should be on fixing what works rather than switching to what has historically failed.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A direct ideological stance from a widely-followed market commentator, relevant context for interpreting his broader political-risk framing of the DSA's midterm momentum.
insights.quote: nothing good comes from, in my opinion, um, socialism over the long run. And we have way too many examples in history to prove that. Um, and capitalism is the model that has brought the greatest amount of prosperity to the far greatest amount of people in human history.

themes.theme: Gold Revaluation: Fiscal Optics vs. Real Fiscal Math

insights.claim: US official gold reserves remain valued on the government's balance sheet at the statutory 1973 price of $42.22/oz under 31 U.S.C. §5116-5117 — roughly 1/100th of the actual market price at the time of taping — and it is legally unclear whether Treasury Secretary Bessent could revalue this administratively or whether it requires an act of Congress.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A concrete legal/statutory fact relevant to any gold-revaluation narrative circulating in markets — the mechanism is contested and would likely trigger an immediate legal fight if attempted.
insights.quote: gold stock that we have in the country is valued at $42 an ounce, right? Not 40. It's 4222 to be exact.

insights.claim: Even a full mark-to-market revaluation of US gold reserves would unlock only about $1 trillion in balance-sheet value — trivial ('left pocket change') against a roughly $40 trillion national debt and annual deficits that alone exceed that amount — meaning the move would change accounting optics but not the actual fiscal trajectory or deficit math.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Directly debunks a popular gold-bug narrative that gold revaluation could meaningfully improve US fiscal solvency — quantifies why it would be a rounding error against total debt and deficits.
insights.quote: If I if I revalue gold and then spend all of that to pay down the debt, I'm I'm not 40 trillion down to 39 trillion. What have I done?

insights.claim: Over the last 30 years, only five governments have used gold-reserve revaluation for fiscal gains — Germany, Italy, Lebanon, Curaçao, and South Africa — a list Lance characterizes as fiscally stressed, non-reserve-currency issuers, implying a US revaluation move today would likely be read internationally as a signal of dollar/fiscal distress rather than a neutral bookkeeping fix, and Treasury has repeatedly declined to pursue it even amid record gold prices and active 2025 proposals.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A historical-precedent-based argument for why a US gold revaluation would carry significant reputational/dollar-confidence risk disproportionate to its trivial fiscal benefit — a reason to discount the likelihood of this policy actually happening.
insights.quote: over the last 30 years only five governments have used reserve revaluation gains. It was Germany, Italy, Lebanon, uh, Kuracal and South Africa. That's not a list of reserve currency issuers that you want to join.

insights.claim: Any realized gold-revaluation gain, if deployed (e.g., placed in the Treasury General Account and used to buy bonds), would functionally expand the money supply and be inflationary, since 'all money is lent into existence' — meaning a naive 'mark gold to market' proposal ignores the actual monetary mechanics of what happens to that newly recognized value.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Clarifies the actual transmission mechanism by which a gold revaluation could become inflationary if spent, correcting a common simplification in popular gold-revaluation commentary.
insights.quote: If you revalue the gold, you literally print money because you just took something at this value and created this value out of it. So now you're actually inflating the monetary supply which is going to be, you know, kind of an issue.

insights.claim: No independent physical audit of official US gold reserves has occurred in decades, leaving the government's precise holdings effectively unverified; Senator Rand Paul recently visited a storage site but this does not constitute a formal audit.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A durable, unresolved transparency gap in US reserve accounting that keeps recurring in gold-revaluation and fiscal-credibility debates — worth tracking if any formal audit effort gains traction.
insights.quote: haven't had a physical audit on the gold, right? So there's there's this kind of question is is all the gold that we say we have actually
